blocks.markdown: What creditors must disclose, when, and how the cost is computed

In this lesson you will: **(1)** enumerate the seven Sec. 4 disclosure items; **(2)** apply the 'prior to consummation' timing rule; **(3)** express finance charges in pesos and as an annual rate, including the BSP effective interest rate (EIR); and **(4)** use *Sampaguita v. PNB* to deny effect to undisclosed charges. This is the most computation-heavy TILA topic — your accounting training is the advantage.

Every creditor must furnish **each borrower**, **before the transaction is consummated**, a **clear written statement** of the seven items (to the extent applicable, per Board rules). Memorize the flow: **price → down payment → difference → non-credit charges → amount financed → peso charge → annual rate**. Items (6) and (7) express the SAME finance charge two ways: absolute (pesos and centavos) and relative (simple annual rate on the outstanding balance). **Practical application:** this statement is the disclosure statement attached to loan contracts — audit it like a working paper: every peso of borrowing cost must be traceable to it.

Timing is **substantive**, not a technicality. Disclosure must come early enough to inform the borrower's consent — *before* consummation. In *UCPB v. Beluso* the bank handed over copies of the promissory notes **after** execution; the Supreme Court held that is **not substantial compliance**: 'The belated discovery of the true cost of credit will too often not be able to reverse the ill effects of an already consummated business decision.' BSP Circular No. 730 repeats the command: banks must furnish each borrower a copy of the disclosure statement **prior to consummation**.

blocks.markdown: Sec. 5 is the statutory basis of all BSP disclosure regulation: the Monetary Board issues the rules, classifications, and differentiations needed to carry out the Act and **prevent circumvention or evasion**. BSP Circular No. 730 (MORB §§X305/X307) is the exercise of this power you must know: it keeps the statute's substance while modernizing computation and disclosure for current banking practice.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: MORB amendments under MB Resolution No. 1018

blocks.markdown: For **small business, retail, and consumer credit**, the BSP requires at minimum: **(1)** total amount to be financed; **(2)** finance charges in pesos and centavos; **(3)** NET PROCEEDS of the loan; and **(4)** the rate as a simple annual rate **or EIR**. General rule: loan terms are disclosed to **all** borrower types. **Accounting relevance:** net proceeds (amount financed minus up-front deductions) is the cash actually received — the present-value anchor of the EIR computation.

The **simple annual rate** assumes an idealized loan: one year, single payment at maturity, no up-front deductions. Real loans differ — so the **EIR must be calculated and disclosed** as the true cost comparable to that benchmark. The EIR follows the PAS definition: the rate that exactly discounts estimated future cash flows over the loan's life to the **net loan proceeds**. In accountancy terms, it is the loan's internal rate of return — the same effective-interest method used for amortized-cost financial instruments. Monthly-contract loans may quote EIR monthly alongside the contractual rate.

blocks.markdown: Banks may charge interest **only on the outstanding balance at the beginning** of each interest or installment period. Repayment schedules and even **marketing materials** must be consistent with this. Effect: flat/add-on rate presentations that understate true cost are out — interest on money already repaid is not allowed. When a problem gives an amortization schedule, verify that each period's interest is computed on the beginning balance.

Disclosure is also **public**: banks must post the disclosure-statement information conspicuously in offices and branches, with explicit notice that the statement is a **required attachment to the loan contract** and that the customer has the **right to demand a copy**. A borrower who never received a copy is a borrower whose right was denied — frame exam answers in those terms.

blocks.markdown: Apply *Sampaguita* in three steps: **(1)** compare the disclosure statement against what the creditor now collects — any interest, penalty, or charge **not revealed there cannot be given effect**, even if the promissory note stipulates it; **(2)** remember the hierarchy — the disclosure statement reflects true cost and is **not a contract the note can novate** (novation is never presumed); **(3)** charges raised without prior notice and consent (here, penalty spiked to 36%) can be struck down or **equitably reduced to zero** as iniquitous. Only the disclosed 19.5% and 21.5% effective rates survived — and PNB refunded P3,686,101.52 in overcollections.

blocks.markdown: **Trap:** when the promissory note and the disclosure statement conflict, the note does **not** win. The statement is the written reflection of true cost; *Sampaguita* refuses to let a later note novate it. Collectibility follows the disclosure statement, not the bolder document.

blocks.markdown: **Exam:** for any disclosure problem, run this checklist: (1) seven Sec. 4 items present? (2) finance charge in BOTH pesos and annual rate? (3) furnished BEFORE consummation? (4) BSP extras for covered loans — net proceeds, EIR, outstanding-balance interest? (5) every collected charge traceable to the statement? A 'no' at any step is a violation with a collectibility consequence.
